what: A pre-brief planning form shown before every PCI lab scenario, with one field per step of Brilakis's fourteen-step plan: baseline monitoring, drugs given, access site and sheath size, guide shape and size, angiographic plan and contrast ceiling (below 3.7 × GFR, lower in CKD, counting recent contrast), target lesion and its ACC/AHA and SCAI class, wire, expected lesion preparation, stent, closure, physiology, imaging, haemodynamic support, and the two or three complications judged most likely with the equipment for each.
learnerDoes: Completes the form from the scenario's chart and films before the case starts; the form stays visible during the case.
success: The debrief scores the form against the scenario: guide size compatible with the lesion preparation actually needed (for example 7 Fr when atherectomy or V-stenting/simultaneous kissing stents are needed), contrast ceiling set and respected, imaging planned when the target was stented before, and the complication that occurred named in advance with its equipment available.

what: Contrast and radiation counters with planned limits: the lab tracks contrast volume against the ceiling written in the pre-brief and cumulative air kerma, raising high-contrast-volume and high-radiation-dose events as each limit approaches (Brilakis: usually stop above 5–7 Gy air kerma; over 15 Gy is a sentinel event; Oxford: radiographer warning at 1 Gy, dose recorded and discussed with the patient).
learnerDoes: Chooses at each warning whether to finish, stage or stop, and records the dose.
success: No case exceeds the learner's own contrast ceiling without an explicit decision; the dose is recorded when the 1 Gy warning is given.

what: Full procedure lab chart with one planted problem per generated patient, drawn from the manuals' checklists: a DOAC taken too recently for its creatinine clearance (Brilakis Table 1.2; Oxford's general 24-hour hold, 72 hours for dabigatran in renal impairment, accepted where the unit protocol follows it), warfarin with an INR not checked within 24 hours, metformin in CKD, a previous contrast reaction without premedication, sildenafil in the past 24 hours or tadalafil in the past 48 hours, an anchor-and-collagen-plug closure device in one groin within 90 days, a dialysis fistula arm, bloods older than 14 days for an out-patient, a planned non-cardiac operation within 6–12 months, an unsuspended do-not-resuscitate order, or a pregnancy test not done.
learnerDoes: Reads the chart before the time-out and chooses the action for each problem (hold and delay, choose another access site, premedicate, avoid nitroglycerin, repeat bloods, rethink stenting, clarify resuscitation status).
success: The planted problem is found and acted on before the time-out is completed; missing it produces the consequence in the case (bleeding, contrast reaction, nitrate hypotension, kidney injury) and the debrief links to the lesson.

what: A scored consent conversation in the full procedure lab whose risks come from the generated patient: Oxford's approximate diagnostic and PCI figures as a starting point, raised by the patient's own factors (age, left main or three-vessel disease, poor LV function, class IV heart failure, aortic valve disease, CKD for kidney injury), with the chance of success, the alternatives (medical therapy, CABG), the long-term risks (restenosis, stent thrombosis, DAPT), the ad hoc plan, and resuscitation status and any proxy.
learnerDoes: Chooses what to tell the patient from a set of statements, including what will and will not be done ad hoc.
success: Mortality is mentioned; patient-specific risk factors are named; alternatives and long-term risks are covered; an ad hoc limit is agreed; a lack of capacity is handled by best interests unless someone holds legal authority.

what: An end-of-diagnostic decision point in the cath lab: the angiogram reveals anatomy beyond what was consented (left main, multivessel disease or a chronic occlusion), and the learner must decide whether to proceed ad hoc or stop.
learnerDoes: Chooses to proceed or to stop, and if stopping, what to arrange (heart-team discussion, a new consent conversation).
success: Ad hoc PCI is declined when the consent does not cover the anatomy or the disease is complex; the debrief cites Brilakis's reasons to delay PCI.

what: A classify-the-lesion step on real angiogram runs that carry expert lesion boxes (CADICA): after locating the lesion, the learner records length (under 10, 10–20, over 20 mm), shape, contour, calcium, angulation, side-branch involvement, ostial position, thrombus and patency, and the app derives the ACC/AHA type (A, B1, B2, C) and SCAI class (I–IV).
learnerDoes: Classifies each lesion with its reasons, then compares with an expert classification where one exists.
success: Agreement with the expert on the type C features and on patency, which together decide the SCAI class.

what: Left main and heavily calcified scenarios in the PCI lab whose set-up depends on the plan: a left main bifurcation case where a 7 or 8 Fr guide, defibrillator pads, a vasopressor plan, intravascular ultrasound and a haemodynamic assessment must be chosen before the start (hypotension follows otherwise; support is chosen from LV function and haemodynamics, not routinely), and a calcified LAD where a 6 Fr radial guide forces a guide exchange when atherectomy is needed.
learnerDoes: Prepares the case from the pre-brief, then manages the consequences of the choices made.
success: Pads, a vasopressor plan and a 7–8 Fr guide are in place for the left main case; the guide chosen for the calcified case accepts the plaque-modification device without an exchange.
